e.etymology: A modern American variant of Cason, a surname used as a first name, in the rhyming family of Mason and Jason. The K spellings took off in the 2010s.
From French Clémentine, the feminine of Clement, from Latin clemens, merciful. Americans know it from the folk ballad Oh My Darling, Clementine and from the small citrus fruit.
namesakes: Clementine Churchill (wife of Winston Churchill)
Clementine Kruczynski (Kate Winslet in Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind)

assoc.t: clementine, the small seedless citrus fruit
Oh My Darling, Clementine, American folk ballad
Clementine, heroine of Telltale's The Walking Dead games

e.etymology: The Arabic form of Joseph, from Hebrew Yosef, he will add. Yusuf is a prophet in the Quran, where a whole chapter tells his story.
namesakes: Yusuf Islam (singer formerly known as Cat Stevens)

e.etymology: From Welsh Maredudd, traditionally read as great lord. Long a men's name in Wales, it became mainly a girls' name in the US during the 20th century.
namesakes: Meredith Grey (lead surgeon of Grey's Anatomy)
Meredith Vieira (TV journalist and host)
Meredith Baxter (actress, Family Ties)

assoc.t: Meredith Grey, title surgeon of Grey's Anatomy

e.etymology: From the English name of the Italian capital, Latin Roma, which Roman legend derived from its founder Romulus. As a first name it sits close to Roman and Romeo.

assoc.t: Rome, capital of Italy and of the ancient Roman Empire

e.etymology: The Spanish, Portuguese and Italian form of Leander, from Greek Leandros, joining leon, lion, and aner, man. In Greek myth Leander swam the Hellespont each night to reach his love, Hero.
A spelling of Amira, from Arabic amira, princess, the feminine of amir, prince.
The French spelling of Killian, an English form of Irish Cillian, a saint's name often linked to cill, church. French soccer star Kylian Mbappé carried the spelling worldwide.
namesakes: Kylian Mbappé (French World Cup-winning soccer star)

assoc.t: Kylian Mbappé, French soccer superstar

e.etymology: An English spelling of Spanish Alonso, a form of Alfonso, a Visigothic name usually read as noble and ready. It was well used in the US in the 1800s.
namesakes: Alonzo Mourning (Hall of Fame NBA center)
Alonzo Harris (Denzel Washington's corrupt detective in Training Day)

e.etymology: From the English word major, the military rank, from Latin for greater. There is also an older English surname Major, from the Norman personal name Mauger.

assoc.t: major, a military officer rank
major, a college student's field of study
Major, the Biden family's German shepherd

e.note: Reads as a military rank or title, so it can cause mix-ups on forms and in introductions.

e.etymology: A modern American variant of Cason, a surname used as a first name, in the rhyming family of Mason and Jason.
From the month, Latin Aprilis, whose own origin is uncertain; one theory ties it to Aphrodite. Used as a name since the early 1900s, it was the top month name for American girls from 1960 to 2000.
namesakes: April O'Neil (reporter in Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles)
April Ludgate (Aubrey Plaza's character on Parks and Recreation)

assoc.t: April, the fourth month, and April Fools' Day

e.etymology: Matches the Hawaiian word makai, toward the sea, used in Hawaii when giving directions. As an American boys' name it also extends Kai and echoes Mekhi and Malachi.
From Latin Lucianus, usually taken as a derivative of the Roman name Lucius, from lux, light. Lucian of Samosata was a Greek satirist of the 2nd century.

assoc.t: Lucian, a champion in the game League of Legends

e.etymology: A modern invention that blends Jasmine with the -lyn ending.
From Greek Kalliope, beautiful voice. In Greek myth Calliope is the muse of epic poetry; the steam organ of circuses and riverboats was named for her.
namesakes: Callie Torres (Calliope, surgeon on Grey's Anatomy)

assoc.t: calliope, the steam organ of circuses and riverboats

e.note: People who have only seen it written often say KAL-ee-ohp.

e.etymology: The Spanish and Portuguese form of Roderick, from a Gothic name meaning famous ruler. Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar is the medieval Spanish hero El Cid.

assoc.t: Olivia Rodrigo, pop singer-songwriter

e.etymology: A medieval English form of Piers, the Old French version of Peter, from Greek petros, rock. Modern use also draws on the surname Pierce.
namesakes: Pierce Brosnan (actor who played James Bond)

assoc.t: Hawkeye Pierce, Alan Alda's surgeon on M*A*S*H
pierce, the verb meaning to puncture

e.etymology: The Cornish form of Guinevere, Welsh Gwenhwyfar, usually read as white phantom or fair and smooth. Rare outside Cornwall before 1900, it was the top US girls' name from 1970 to 1984.
namesakes: Jennifer Lopez (singer and actress)
Jennifer Aniston (actress, Friends)
Jennifer Lawrence (Oscar-winning actress)

e.etymology: A French feminine diminutive of Jacques, the French form of Jacob and James, from Hebrew Ya'akov, tied to the word for heel because Jacob was born grasping his twin Esau's heel.
namesakes: Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis (First Lady)

e.etymology: From Spanish Anahí, taken from the Guarani name of the ceibo, or cockspur coral tree, whose red blossom is the national flower of Argentina and Uruguay.
namesakes: Anahí (Mexican singer and actress of the group RBD)

assoc.t: Anahí, Mexican singer and actress of RBD

e.etymology: The French feminine form of Gabriel, from Hebrew Gavri'el, God is my strong one. Gabriel is the archangel who announces the births of John the Baptist and Jesus.
namesakes: Gabrielle Union (actress)
Gabrielle Chanel (fashion designer known as Coco Chanel)
Gabrielle Douglas (Olympic gymnast Gabby Douglas)

e.etymology: From Hebrew Moshe through Greek and Latin. Exodus explains it as drawn out of the water; scholars often suggest an Egyptian root meaning to give birth, as in names like Ramesses.
namesakes: Moses (prophet who led the Israelites out of Egypt)
Moses Malone (Hall of Fame NBA center)

assoc.t: Moses, the Biblical prophet of the Ten Commandments

e.etymology: From Hawaiian Nālani, joining nā, the plural form of the, with lani, sky or heaven. It can be read as the heavens or the chiefs.
A spelling of Hannah, from Hebrew Channah, grace. Hanna is the standard form in Scandinavia, Germany, Poland and Finland. In the Bible Hannah is the mother of the prophet Samuel.
namesakes: Hanna Marin (Ashley Benson's character on Pretty Little Liars)

assoc.t: Hanna, teen assassin of the 2011 film and Amazon series

e.etymology: A modern American variant of Cason, a surname used as a first name, in the rhyming family of Mason and Jason.
A modern respelling of Cason, a surname used as a first name, in the style of Mason, Jason and Grayson.

e.meaning: from a Roman family name, possibly from Latin caecus, blind
e.etymology: A spelling variant of Cecilia, from Latin Caecilia, the feminine of the Roman family name Caecilius, possibly from caecus, blind. Saint Cecilia, a Roman martyr, is the patron saint of music.

assoc.t: Simon & Garfunkel's 1970 song Cecilia (same sound)

e.etymology: From Hebrew Shet, appointed or placed, by way of Greek. In Genesis, Seth is the third son of Adam and Eve, born after the death of Abel.
namesakes: Seth Rogen (actor and comedian)
Seth Meyers (late-night TV host)
Seth MacFarlane (creator of Family Guy)

assoc.t: Egyptian god of chaos and storms, also spelled Set

e.meaning: from a Roman family name, long linked to Latin virgo, maiden
e.etymology: From the Roman family name Verginius, later tied to Latin virgo, maiden. The colony of Virginia was named for Elizabeth I, the Virgin Queen, and Virginia Dare was the first English child born there, in 1587.
namesakes: Virginia Woolf (English novelist)
Virginia Dare (first English child born in the American colonies)

assoc.t: US state on the Atlantic coast
Yes, Virginia, there is a Santa Claus (1897 editorial)

e.note: The first two syllables sound like the word virgin, an easy target for schoolyard teasing.

e.etymology: In Swahili, amani is the word for peace, itself borrowed from Arabic aman, safety. As an Arabic name, Amani means wishes or aspirations.

e.meaning: from the Roman family name Aemilius, traditionally read as rival
e.etymology: A spelling of Emilia, from the Roman family name Aemilius, traditionally linked to Latin aemulus, rival. It is often blended with Amelia, a separate Germanic name.
